s: Vanilla features that are switched off in the Caeldun Isles, and why.
x: Settlers III is about slow progress and real distance. A few vanilla features would undo that in an afternoon, so they're switched off. All of these are enforced in game. Banned What happens Elytra Elytra won't open. You can wear one, but you can't glide. The Nether Nether portals won't light, and existing portals don't take you anywhere. The End End portals don't take you anywhere. Ice-boat highways Ice, packed ice and blue ice can't be placed. Placing water Water can't be poured from a bucket or a dispenser. Lava can't either. Elytra Flight would make the size of the world meaningless. Gliding is cancelled the moment it starts, so elytra are decoration at best. To cover distance, build roads, ride horses or sail. See Ships. The Nether The Nether is sealed. Portal frames won't light, so there's no Nether travel (which would cut every journey to an eighth), no Nether fortresses, and no blaze rods or wither skeletons. The only fire-and-brimstone in the world is on the Burning Isle, and you'll need a ship to reach it. The End The End is sealed too. That's also why there are no elytra, shulker boxes from End cities, or dragon eggs. Ice-boat highways Boats on packed or blue ice travel faster than almost anything in vanilla, which would turn the long journeys between regions into a few minutes. Ice, packed ice and blue ice can't be placed, so the highways can't be built. Natural ice on frozen water is untouched. Placing water and lava You can't create water. Buckets won't pour it, dispensers won't place it, and ice won't melt into it. Lava and powder snow are blocked the same way. You can still fill a bucket from a river or loch, fill water bottles to drink, and fill cauldrons. This means: Farms go where the water is. Farmland needs water nearby, so fields sit beside rivers, burns and lochs, not wherever you like. See Farming. No infinite water sources, water elevators or bucket-clutch tricks. No lava casts or lava traps. If you want water somewhere, you have to dig a channel to bring it there. See also How Settlers plays.

s: A huge archipelago of rain-washed islands, sea lochs and mountains, shaped from real survey data.
x: The map The world of Settlers III is the Caeldun Isles, an Atlantic archipelago of long outer islands, mountainous inner isles, small islands on the edge of the abyss, low fertile farming isles and wooded peninsulas. The land is shaped from real survey height data, so its hills, glens, sea lochs and coastlines look and feel like real ones. (Where the look comes from.) Size 32,768 × 45,056 blocks Scale 1 block ≈ 4 real metres across, and about the same vertically Regions 15, grouped into 5 lands (see Lands & regions) Highest ground Mountain tops approach Y 300; the highest peak, in Morvethan, reaches about Y 306 Current status The whole map has been generated and is being prepared. For now settlers play in the individual regional worlds, starting on Tirwenn. The rules on this wiki apply in both. Travel is slow on purpose Crossing the map on foot takes a very long time, and that's the design. Distance is what gives regions their own character and makes trade worth doing. Expect to rely on: Roads. Paths wear into the ground where people walk. See The living world. Horses. Wild horses and donkeys roam the Outer Isles. Ships. The only way across the open sea, and the only way to move serious cargo. See Ships & sailing. The weight system (see Weight) means you can't carry a quarry's worth of stone in your pockets either. What the land looks like Biomes are fewer and more realistic than vanilla. You'll find: Atlantic rainforest: oak woodland dripping with ivy, ferns and moss, with bluebells, ramsons and foxgloves on the floor. Old pinewood: big pines over heather and blaeberry, with juniper thickets. Machair and white sand: the turquoise-water beaches of the western isles. Heather moor and bare gneiss: open, windswept, nearly treeless outer islands. Mountain glens: burns cascading down incised gorges, peat-dark lochs, crags and boulder fields. Sea cliffs: sheer east-facing cliffs on the outer islands, with gravel and shingle beaches below. Water inland is dark and peaty. The sea turns turquoise over the shallows near land and drops to deep blue over the abyss offshore. Snow Snow only lies on the very highest summits. The snowline gets lower the further north you go: about 3 blocks lower for every kilometre north. In the pinewoods of Ardveil it comes down to around Y 205. Caves Caves are rarer than in vanilla and they never break open on a hillside by accident. Entrances are few, mossy and easy to miss. Inside are tubes, caverns and occasional great halls with dripstone, streams in the floor, and flooding at depth. Only the Northlands have lava in their caves, along with amethyst, sulfur and cinnabar veins.

s: Every command an ordinary player can use, on one page.
x: Getting around Command What it does /spawn Go to your spawn point. /sethome Set your home where you stand. You get one. /home Go home. /delhome Remove your home. /backdeath Return to where you last died. Teleports make you stand still for 5 seconds (moving or being hit cancels them) and have a 60-second cooldown. Survival Command What it does /stats Show your protein, fruit and veg, grains and thirst. See Nutrition. /needs hud on|off Show or hide the needs bar. Ships Command What it does /ship create <name> Make the block you're looking at a ship's wheel. /ship menu The wheel menu for the ship you're on. /ship board Join a ship's crew. /ship leave Leave the crew. /ship dock Drop anchor. /ship list Your ships and where they are. /ship remove Stop a build being a ship (the blocks stay). /ship Help. At sea: W/S throttle, A/D steer, sneak twice to get off. See Ships. Shops Command What it does /shop create <name> Open a shop where you stand. /shop list Your shops. /shop <name> Stock, gold and owners. /shop <name> add|remove <player> Manage co-owners. /shop <name> move Move the keeper to you. /shop <name> rename <new> Rename the shop. /shop <name> skin Change the keeper's look. /shop <name> delete Close the shop (empty it first). /shop help Help. See Gold & shops. Chat and social Command What it does /msg <player> <message> Private message. /r <message> Reply to your last message. /mail Leave a message for someone who's offline. /me <action> Describe an action in chat. /list Who's online. /afk Mark yourself away. /helpop <message> Ask the admins for help. /rules Server rules. s: Where each crop will grow in the Caeldun Isles. Potato and beetroot grow everywhere; pumpkins only on the Spiderholme Isles.
x: Each colour shows arable ground where that crop will grow. Tick crops on and off below the map. Crop summary Crop Where it grows Arable land Potato Everywhere, at full speed 82.0% Beetroot Everywhere, at full speed 82.0% Wheat The Breadbasket at full speed; the Rainlands at 1% speed 31.3% Carrot The Breadbasket only 3.2% Pumpkin The Spiderholme Isles only: Ruannis, Maigor and Cannoch 1.9% Melon The Breadbasket only 3.2% Sugar cane The Breadbasket only, right beside water 0.4% "Arable land" is the share of all land where that crop can be farmed. Most of the wheat country on the map is Rainlands ground, where wheat grows at a hundredth of normal speed. Only a small share of the world grows grain properly. These rules are enforced in game: a crop won't grow outside the lands listed here, and bone meal won't help. See Farming & crops.

s: Items and recipes that work differently from vanilla, starting with whale blubber.
x: Settlers III adds a handful of its own items and changes a few recipes. This page lists each one. Whale blubber Source Whales in the deep ocean (the abyss offshore) Works like Vanilla honeycomb, in every way Whale blubber is thick fat cut from a whale. It does everything honeycomb does in vanilla: Waxing copper. Use blubber on any copper block, door, trapdoor, grate or bulb to wax it, so it never oxidises. Waxed copper also stays at full strength, since oxidised copper is structurally weaker (see Gravity). Waxing signs so nobody can edit them. Candles: string and blubber make a candle. Blubber blocks: four blubber make a block (vanilla's honeycomb block). Beehives and anything else that uses honeycomb in a recipe. Getting it means sailing out to deep water. Whales are curious and will come to look at your ship, but they drift away if you hurt them. See The open ocean. Trade good Candlelight and waxed copper are wanted everywhere, and only sailors can get blubber. That makes it a natural export for coastal settlements with a ship. Rails The rail recipe (six iron ingots and a stick) makes 32 rails instead of vanilla's 16. Rail lines are one of the few ways to move people and goods over land quickly, and iron is scarce outside the Rainlands, so rails go further here. Feathers Chickens drop 2–3 feathers (vanilla drops 0–2), and wild birds such as robins, finches and gulls drop 3–6. Chickens only live on the Spiderholme Isles, so everywhere else, fletchers rely on birds. Sand Natural sand drops nothing when broken. Sand comes from panning gravel streams with a bowl, which also turns up gold and iron nuggets and flint. Gold as money Gold nuggets, bars and blocks are the currency, traded through player-run shop keepers. See Gold & shops. Trees fall Chopping through a trunk fells the whole tree, and saplings grow into the region's own trees. See Tree felling. For things that have been switched off entirely, see Banned & changed.

s: Money is real gold you carry. Players run the shops, through shop keepers that trade one item each.
x: Gold is money There's no virtual balance. Gold is the currency, carried in your inventory: Unit Worth 1 gold block 9 bars = 81 nuggets 1 gold bar (ingot) 9 nuggets 1 gold nugget 1 nugget Only plain gold counts. Renamed or enchanted gold doesn't. Change is given automatically, so if you pay with a bar for a 3-nugget item, you get 6 nuggets back. Gold comes from the Outer Isles, where it's in the rock, and from panning streams anywhere. Because money has to be mined or panned, it's genuinely scarce. Using a shop Shops are run by shop keepers: NPCs that stand where their owner put them. Right-click one to trade. Selling shops sell you an item. Click a price to buy. Items may come in bundles of 1, 8 or 64. Buying shops buy an item from you. Click to sell them your goods for gold. A purchase only goes through if everything fits in your inventory, so nothing is dropped or lost. Running your own shop Stand where you want the keeper and run /shop create <name>. Right-click your keeper to set it up: Pick the item by clicking it in your inventory. Each shop trades one item. Choose the mode: Selling (you sell to customers) or Buying (you buy from them). Set prices by clicking the blocks, bars and nuggets: left-click adds one, right-click takes one off. Choose which bundles to offer: 1s, and optionally 8s and 64s. Selling: add stock, and come back to collect your takings. Buying: deposit gold for the keeper to pay with, and collect what it has bought. Stock and gold are held by the keeper, not in chests, so nobody can break in and take them. A shop holds up to 1,728 items (27 stacks) of stock. Co-owners A shop can have several owners. Any owner can restock, set prices and collect. Only the founder can close the shop, and it has to be empty first. Limits Up to 5 shops per player. Prices go up to 99 gold blocks. Shop commands /shop create <name> Open a shop where you stand. /shop list Your shops. /shop <name> Stock, gold and owners. /shop <name> add <player> Add a co-owner. /shop <name> remove <player> Remove a co-owner. /shop <name> move Move the keeper to where you are. /shop <name> rename <new> Rename the shop. /shop <name> skin Change the keeper's look. /shop <name> delete Close the shop (empty it first). /shop help All of the above, in game. Trade between lands Shops make most sense where the trade routes meet. A Breadbasket farmer selling bread, a Rainlands smith buying coal, or a harbour-side keeper buying diamonds off Outer Isles miners are all how the world's economy is meant to work. See Lands & regions for who has what.

s: Crops grow differently in every land. Potato and beetroot grow everywhere; everything else is regional.
x: Like ores, crops are regional. Each land has a list of what will grow there. Anything not on the list won't grow at all, and some crops on the list grow slowly. What grows where Crop Outer Isles Northlands Spiderholme Breadbasket Rainlands Wheat ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ 1% speed Potato ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Beetroot ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Carrot ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ Pumpkin ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✗ Melon ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ Sugar cane ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ Enforced in game A crop won't grow outside the lands listed for it, and bone meal won't force it. Rainlands wheat keeps only 1 growth step in 100. Farms in the wrong land simply stop growing. You can't place water Water can't be poured from buckets or dispensers (see Banned & changed), so fields have to sit beside natural rivers, burns, ponds and lochs, or on a channel you've dug from one. Why it matters Bread is the main source of grains, and grains are one of your four nutrition meters. Outside the Breadbasket, nobody can grow wheat properly. The Rainlands can technically grow it, but a wheat field there takes a hundred times as long. That makes Breadbasket farmers some of the most important people in the world. Every land can grow potatoes and beetroot at full speed, so everyone eats well for fruit and veg, and on hunting and fishing for protein. They just need to buy their bread. Sugar cane Sugar cane follows vanilla's rule: the block it stands on needs water directly beside it at the same level. On Tirwenn it grows wild along pond edges and streams. Animals Livestock is regional too. Chickens live only in the Spiderholme Isles. Sheep, horses and donkeys roam wild on the Outer Isles, and the Breadbasket is cattle, pig and chicken country. If you want a mixed farm, you'll have to bring animals home by ship. Ships carry penned animals safely, and horses have been tested at sea. See Ships. Trees and saplings Trees grow back. Saplings drop a little more often than in vanilla, and in the Caeldun worlds a sapling grows into the region's own tree shape rather than a vanilla one. A pine sapling in Ardveil grows into a proper tall pine, not a vanilla spruce. Saplings need light (level 9 or more) and take about 20 minutes on average. See Tree felling.

s: Cut through the trunk and the whole tree comes down. Watch where it lands.
h: When you break a log without felling
x: Trees fall like trees. Chop through the trunk of a natural tree with an axe and everything above the cut topples away from you and crashes to the ground. How it works Break a log low on a natural tree with an axe and the rest of the trunk and crown falls. The logs land as a lying trunk you can then cut up. Some logs splinter into sticks (up to 3 per tree). Most of the crown shatters as it hits the ground, dropping sticks and saplings. What's left decays over the next minute or so. Felling costs your axe 2 extra durability on top of the normal wear. Sneak while chopping to take a single log the ordinary way. Timber! A falling trunk does 6 damage (3 hearts) to anything it lands on, you included. Stand to the side. Limits A felled tree can be up to 160 logs and 40 blocks tall above the cut. Bushes and tiny trees (fewer than 2 logs above the cut) are chopped normally. Trees you've built yourself from placed leaves don't fell; only natural ones do. When you break a log without felling If you remove logs the ordinary way, leaves that are no longer attached to anything fall away over about 25 seconds, as a real crown would. Leaves you placed yourself never fall. Regrowth Leaves drop saplings a bit more often than in vanilla. In the Caeldun worlds, a sapling grows into the tree that belongs to the region, not a vanilla tree. Spruce saplings grow into proper tall pines, dark oak into alder or holly, jungle saplings into palms, and flowering azalea into rowan. Saplings need light level 9 or more and take about 20 minutes on average to grow. Bone meal works on saplings too, and grows the same regional tree. Woodland slowly reseeds itself near existing trees. See The living world.

s: Which trees grow where across the Caeldun Isles, and how thick the woods are.
x: Each colour is one kind of tree. The stronger the colour, the more trees per chunk; a full wood is about 7 per chunk. Tick species on and off below the map. Tree summary Tree Where it grows Found on Densest stands Grows from Oak The oakwoods of Sgorrachan and the ancient woods of the Rainlands 40.5% 6.5 per chunk Oak sapling Pine The great pinewoods of Ardveil and Dùnross 20.4% 5.6 per chunk Spruce sapling Birch Mixed through the woods, especially near water 25.5% 3.8 per chunk Birch sapling Holly Understorey of the oakwoods 8.4% 3.8 per chunk Dark oak sapling Alder Low, wet ground in the Spiderholme fern country 0.3% 3.1 per chunk Dark oak sapling Rowan Scattered widely, never in dense stands 46.7% 1.3 per chunk Flowering azalea Palm Sheltered spots on the Breadbasket coast 3.2% 0.34 per chunk Jungle sapling "Found on" is the share of all land where that tree grows at all. What it means The Outer Isles have almost no trees. Settlers there import timber, or build in stone and turf. Timber is the best structural material for its reach (see Gravity), so the wooded lands have a builder's advantage. Saplings grow into the region's own tree shapes. See Tree felling.

s: Where you arrive, what you carry, and how to survive your first few days in the Caeldun Isles.
x: Joining Settlers III runs on Minecraft Java Edition. The server supports recent client versions, but for the best experience use the current release. While the server is in testing, the address is shared directly with players. Ask an admin for it. When you join, the server offers you a resource pack. Accept it. It supplies the region's plants, animals and textures: bluebells, foxgloves and wild orchids, red deer, grouse, mosquitoes and whales. Without it, a lot of creatures will look like the vanilla animal they're built on (a red deer will look like a camel). Where you arrive New settlers arrive on a long sand beach on the island of Tirwenn in the Breadbasket, facing south over the bay. Tirwenn is the gentlest place in the world: warm, flat, fertile, and free of wolves, bears and hostile humanoids. It's the place to find your feet before you head out. It's morning when you first arrive, so you have a full day ahead of you. What you carry Every new player gets a one-time starter kit: Armour Chainmail helmet, iron chestplate, chainmail leggings, leather boots Weapons Iron sword, bow, 16 arrows Food 16 bread, 16 apples, 16 cooked beef That food is a balanced diet on purpose: grains, fruit and protein. See Nutrition for why that matters. Mind the water Your starter armour weighs 20 units. Past 30 units of worn armour (about a full iron set) you sink in water. See Weight & encumbrance. Your rank Everyone starts as an Apprentice, shown as [Apprentice] before your name in chat. Useful basics Inventory is kept on death. You won't lose your pack, but dying costs some nutrition. /backdeath takes you back to where you last died. /sethome and /home: you get one home. /spawn returns you to your spawn point. Teleports take 5 seconds of standing still (moving or being hit cancels them) and have a 60-second cooldown. The full list is on the Commands page. Your first days Look at what's around you. Every region has its own ores, crops and animals. Read Lands & regions to see what your region has and what it lacks. Get food going. Tirwenn grows almost every crop: wheat, carrots, melons and sugar cane as well as potatoes and beetroot. Most of the world grows only the last two, so farmers here have something to sell. See Farming. Find water to drink. Thirst falls much faster than hunger. Carry water bottles. Pan for gold. A bowl in a shallow gravel stream can turn up gold nuggets, and gold is money. See Panning. Build with gravity in mind. Your first house needs to hold itself up. See Gravity & building. Plan your first voyage. Sooner or later you'll need something from another island, and you can't swim there. See Ships. Sand can't be gathered by hand Natural beach sand drops nothing when broken, which protects the coastline. Sand comes from panning instead.

s: Place names, old words and server terms you'll meet around the Caeldun Isles.
x: Term Meaning Abyss The deep ocean beyond an island's shelf, more than 40 blocks deep. Deadly to swimmers and small boats. See The open ocean. Apprentice The rank every new player starts with. Blaeberry Bilberry, a low shrub of the pinewood floor. Burn A mountain stream. Burns with gravel beds are where you pan. Caeldun Isles The world of Settlers III. Crag A rocky outcrop. District A rich patch of an ore within its home land. See Resources. Encumbrance Being slowed down by what you carry. See Weight. Glen A long, deep mountain valley. Hang How far below itself a material can hold something up. See Gravity. Helm / wheel The block you steer a ship from. Keeper An NPC that runs a player's shop. Land One of five groups of regions sharing a climate, ores and crops: Outer Isles, Northlands, Spiderholme, Breadbasket, Rainlands. Loch A lake, or a sea inlet. Machair Flat, flowery, sandy grassland behind the beaches of the western isles. Ramsons Wild garlic, carpeting the oakwood floor in spring. Reach How far sideways a material can carry a load. See Gravity. Region One of the fifteen named areas of the map, each with its own character. Shelf The shallow sea around an island, safe for swimming and small boats. Shingle A beach of pebbles and gravel. Most Caeldun beaches are shingle; sand is found in sheltered bays. Spell A stretch of weather lasting 10 to 40 minutes, either wet or bright. See Weather.

s: Anything you build has to hold itself up. Timber carries loads a long way, stone barely overhangs at all, and a badly planned roof comes down.
x: In Settlers III, blocks you place need support. Every placed block has to trace a path back through solid material to the natural ground. If it can't, it cracks, creaks, and after a two-second warning falls. A stone castle is a serious achievement here. The stone is heavy to haul from the quarry, and without well-planned supports it won't stay up. The rules Straight up is free. A column or wall can be any height as long as it stands on something. Sideways costs. Each block of overhang uses up some of the carrying block's reach. When it runs out, the next block falls. Diagonally down works too. Stepping each course out a little (corbelling) is a real technique. Hanging below is hard. Blocks hanging under a support depend on its hang strength. Stone can barely hang anything; chains and iron can. Spans supported at both ends go further. Arches and bridges work because each half helps hold up the middle. The block doing the carrying decides. A stone block on the end of a long oak beam is fine, because the beam still has reach to spare. A stone shelf sticking out of a stone wall runs out after a couple of blocks. Built blocks and dug mines These support rules apply to blocks players have placed. Natural hills, cliffs and caves stay put, but mines you dig can cave in. Material strengths Class Blocks Reach Hang Timber Logs, planks, wooden stairs, slabs and trapdoors, bamboo blocks 12 0 Prop Scaffolding 19 10 Metal Iron, gold, diamond, emerald, lapis and copper blocks; chains; iron bars 19 12 Reinforced Obsidian, netherite blocks, reinforced deepslate 29 15 Lattice Fences, walls, ladders 7 0 Masonry Bricks, polished and smooth stone, sandstone, terracotta, concrete, quartz, deepslate tiles 4 1 Weak masonry Cracked, mossy and chiselled variants 2 0 Stone Stone, deepslate, basalt, ores, most other solid blocks 2 1 Rough stone Cobblestone, andesite, diorite, granite, tuff, blackstone 2 0 Glass All glass 1 0 Soft Wool, carpets, leaves, hay, moss 1 2 Soil Dirt, grass, mud, clay, farmland, snow blocks 0 0 Reach is roughly how many blocks sideways a material can carry a load. Hang is how far below itself it can hold something up. Building techniques that work Timber frames Timber has by far the best reach of any common material. A timber frame with posts and beams can carry a stone infill or a stone floor on top, because the beams do the carrying. Most practical buildings will be timber-framed. Arches and bridges A span supported from both ends gets extra strength, so arches, vaults and bridges are possible even in masonry. Build from both sides and meet in the middle. Props Scaffolding is the prop: cheap, strong, and clearly a support. Use it to hold things up while you build, or leave it in place as permanent shoring. Hanging things To hang a lantern, a chandelier or a floor from above, use chains or iron. They're the only common blocks with real hanging strength. Rafts, docks and jetties Timber floats. Water supports timber for a short distance, so wooden jetties, rafts and pontoons work. Stone gets no help from water: you can't found a keep on a lake. Collapses Before anything falls you'll see cracks spread across it and hear creaking. You have about 2 seconds to get clear. Everything that's lost support falls together. Falling blocks hurt whatever they land on. Blocks break as they land: stone becomes cobblestone, cobblestone becomes gravel, stone bricks crack, grass and dirt become coarse dirt, and glass shatters completely. Timber survives the fall intact. Buildings age Stone brick near water slowly turns mossy and cracked over time (see The living world), and weathered masonry is weaker than fresh. An old building nobody maintains can eventually come down by itself. Oxidised copper is also weaker than fresh copper. Cave-ins Mines you dig into natural rock can collapse. Caves and halls that were already there when the world was made are stable; only the spaces players open are judged. Cave-ins are live on the full Caeldun map. Width is what matters. A tunnel 1 block wide is always safe, however tall, and so is a crossing of two of them. The wider the open span of roof you dig out, the riskier each further block you mine. Height makes wide rooms worse. Up to 3 blocks of headroom is free; beyond that, a wide room gets steadily riskier. Soil roofs are weaker. A roof of dirt, clay or mud is twice as likely to fall as rock. Shallow digs are safe. Roofs with less than 4 blocks of cover above them aren't judged. You're told the risk in chat as you dig. Posts Brace the roof with posts: a column of wooden fence, logs or scaffolding standing on the floor and pressed right up against the rock roof. A post braces the roof within about 4 blocks of it (posts every 8 blocks cover a tunnel). Planks don't count, and a post that stops short of the roof holds nothing. Roof Risk What falls Braced by a post A tenth of normal At most a stone or three No post nearby Up to double Usually a few stones, but sometimes a real collapse of up to 24 blocks Falling rock does 3 damage per block to anyone underneath. You get a crack-and-creak warning first: 1.5 seconds for a small fall, 3 seconds for a big one. Jamming a post in during the warning still saves it. Protected land Collapses respect protected regions and claims. They won't tear through land you aren't allowed to build in.

s: The player guide to Settlers III, a slow, regional survival server set in a rain-washed Atlantic archipelago.
h: The Caeldun Isles · full map page · mining · forestry · crops
x: Welcome to the Settlers III Wiki The player guide to a slow, regional Minecraft survival server set in a rain-washed Atlantic archipelago. The Caeldun Isles · full map page · mining · forestry · crops About Settlers III Settlers III takes its idea from The Settlers I and II: resources are regional and progress is slow. Iron comes from the Rainlands, emerald from the Breadbasket, diamond from the Outer Isles, and wheat will barely grow in half the world. Getting materials from where they are to where you need them is the game. The world is the Caeldun Isles, a huge archipelago of islands, sea lochs and mountains, with Atlantic rainforest, old pinewood, machair and peat-dark lochs. It rains a lot. No elytra farms on day two. Slow progress, real distance and trade between regions will give us an interesting geopolitical situation, without anyone having to roleplay. New here? Getting started: where you arrive, what you carry, your first days How Settlers plays: everything that differs from vanilla, on one page Lands & regions: what each part of the world offers Commands: every player command New settlers arrive on a long sand beach on the warm, gentle island of Tirwenn. The core rules Regional scarcity: every land has its own ores, crops and animals. Nobody is self-sufficient. Weight: carry too much and you slow to a crawl; heavy armour sinks you. Gravity: buildings must hold themselves up. The open ocean: kills swimmers and small boats. Build a ship. Nutrition: protein, fruit and veg, grains and thirst. Gold is money: players run the shops. No shortcuts: no elytra, no Nether, no ice highways, no placing water. s: The rules that make Settlers III different from vanilla survival, on one page.
x: If you've played a lot of vanilla survival, most of your instincts still work. These are the things that don't. Vanilla habit On Settlers III Read more Everything is available everywhere Ores, crops and animals are regional. Your island has some things and not others. Resources Fill your inventory and walk home Weight slows you down, then stops you sprinting, then stops you jumping. Weight Swim or row to the next island The deep ocean kills swimmers and small boats. You need a ship. Open ocean Build a floating roof on four pillars Player-placed blocks need support. Overhangs and wide roofs collapse. Gravity Dig out a big room underground Wide mine roofs cave in unless you brace them with posts. Cave-ins Fly with elytra, use the Nether Elytra won't glide, and the Nether and End are sealed. Banned Build an ice-boat highway Ice can't be placed. Banned Pour water wherever you like Water and lava can't be placed, even from dispensers. Farm by natural water. Banned Chop a tree one log at a time Cut the trunk and the whole tree falls, and it can crush you. Tree felling Hunger bar is all that matters Four meters: protein, fruit and veg, grains, and thirst. Nutrition Emeralds and villagers are money Gold is money: 81 nuggets to the block. Players run the shops. Economy Dig sand off the beach Natural sand drops nothing. Pan for it in streams. Panning Wheat grows anywhere with water Potatoes and beetroot grow everywhere. Wheat, carrots, melons and sugar cane are Breadbasket crops, and pumpkins grow only on the Spiderholme Isles. Farming Weather is occasional It's the Atlantic. It rains about half the time, usually clearing just before sunset. Weather Zombies and creepers everywhere Each region has its own designed wildlife: wolves, bears, deer, crabs, spirits. Wildlife The idea behind it Slow progress is the point. In most servers the first week is a race to diamond gear, elytra and farms, and then there's nothing to do but wait. Here, distance is real and scarcity is regional, so a settlement's wealth depends on where it is, what it can make, and who it trades with. That's meant to produce politics on its own. Whoever controls the only good farmland feeds the world. Whoever holds the iron country equips it. The sea lanes between them matter. You don't need to roleplay any of this; it follows from the rules. What you keep Your inventory on death. Dying costs time and a little nutrition, not your belongings. Vanilla crafting, with a few adjustments (rails craft 32 at a time, for example). Vanilla combat, against a very different set of creatures.

s: Where the look and feel of the Caeldun Isles comes from, and the data it was built with.
x: The Caeldun Isles are a fictional world, but they're drawn from a real place. The look and feel The world is inspired by the Atlantic coast of Scotland: the Hebrides and the western Highlands. That's where the long, low outer islands with their white-sand beaches and turquoise shallows come from, and the mountainous inner isles and their temperate rainforest of oak, ivy, moss and fern. The old pinewoods, the machair, the peat-dark lochs, the tumbling burns, the shingle shores and the weather that rarely stays dry for long all come from there too. Some of the words used on this wiki (burn, glen, loch, machair, blaeberry) come from the same place. The regions of the Caeldun Isles are reinterpretations, not copies. Their names, their resources, their creatures and their character belong to the world of Settlers III. Terrain data The shape of the land was built from real height data and then reworked for the game: coasts redrawn, rivers carved, mountains steepened and the whole map blended into one world. Contains OS data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. Height data from OS Terrain 50, used under the Open Government Licence.

s: Five lands, fifteen regions. Each land has its own climate, ores, crops and animals, and none of them has everything.
x: The Caeldun Isles are divided into five lands. A land decides what grows, what you can dig up and what lives there. Within each land are named regions, each with its own character. Outer Isles Windswept, treeless. Diamond, redstone, a little gold. Northlands Pinewood and mountains. Coal, quartz, amethyst, lava. Spiderholme Isles Fern islands on the abyss. Lapis. The only pumpkins and chickens. Breadbasket Warm and flat. Wheat and most crops. Emerald. Rainlands Ancient oakwood. Rich iron. Wheat barely grows. The Outer Isles Climate Cold and windswept. Almost no trees; heather over bare rock, machair and white-sand beaches in the west, high sea cliffs in the east. Crops Potato and beetroot. Ores Diamond and redstone deep down; gold in a few places, and a little gold anywhere you dig. Trace coal and copper. Animals Wild sheep, wild horses and donkeys, rabbits. Bears and wolves at lower numbers. Barren skeletons and native tribes roam the moors. # Region Character 1 Fearnmuir A long chain of low, loch-riddled islands 2 Dunbarra A rugged island group around the harbour of Castleross 15 The Burning Isle See below. The Northlands Climate Cool, with a low snowline and dense forest: old pinewood in the north, Atlantic oakwood around the jagged southern mountains. Crops Potato and beetroot. Ores Coal is common and quartz fairly common. Amethyst, sulfur and cinnabar veins line the caves. The only lava in the world is here. Iron and copper are very rare. Folded layers of granite, diorite, andesite, tuff and basalt run under the surface. Clay pockets surface as mud in the pinewoods. Animals Wolves (in packs), brown bears, red deer, boar, wild goats, foxes, wildcats, frogs and giant bull frogs by the water, eagles overhead. Spirits haunt the high ground. # Region Character 3 Ardveil Big pine forest under a long ridge of cliffs 4 Dùnross Pinewood, moor and sea lochs in the north-west 5 Sgorrachan Jagged mountains, oak woodland, tumbling burns and a rugged coast 14 Ardcarran A remote peninsula on the eastern mainland. Also has lapis, a little iron and emerald. The Spiderholme Isles Climate Cool and forested like the Northlands. The islands sit on the edge of the abyss: open alder and oak wood low down, fern and grass on the hills. Crops Potato, beetroot and pumpkin. These are the only isles in the world where pumpkins grow. Ores Lapis lazuli, deep. No real coal or iron, only traces. Animals Chickens live here and nowhere else. Here they're black grouse. Giant spiders infest the woods of Maigor. No wolves, no bears. Whales and giant squid in the deep water offshore. # Region Character 6 Ruannis A mountainous island 7 Maigor A small island of cliffs and dark woods 8 Cannoch Fern and alder island at the edge of the abyss The Breadbasket Climate The warmest isles: flat, fertile and sunny by local standards. Golden meadows, sheltered palms and cordylines, sandy coves and hundreds of small ponds. Crops Every crop but pumpkin grows here: wheat, potato, carrot, beetroot, melon and sugar cane. The only place wheat grows at full speed. Ores Emerald, deep. A little copper in pockets, sometimes showing in surface boulders. Coal and iron are extremely rare. Animals Farm country: cattle, chickens and pigs. On the islands themselves, no large predators and no hostile humanoids. Instead there are crabs, toads, newts, foxes, muntjac, island boar, palm spiders, and clouds of mosquitoes and midges. # Region Character 9 Colvane A low, rocky farming island 10 Tirwenn The Golden Coast, where new settlers arrive The Rainlands Climate Milder and wetter, with a higher snowline than the north. Ancient oak wood covers the lowland: huge old trees, deep shade, fallen trunks and mushrooms. Open hills and rocky tops above. Crops Potato and beetroot at full speed. Wheat grows extremely slowly, at 1% of the normal rate. Ores Rich in iron, at vanilla levels. Copper and coal are very low. Animals Wolves, brown bears, red deer, boar, wild goats, foxes, frogs and newts. Spirits on the high ground. # Region Character 11 Morvethan The most mountainous region, with the highest peak in the world 12 Ionfarr Ancient oakwood over a long, low peninsula 13 Ardnamor A wild peninsula reaching out to the west The Burning Isle At the far northern end of the Outer Isles lies an island unlike anything else in the Caeldun Isles. Sheer cliffs about 60 blocks high ring the coast. Inland, the grass gives way to cinders, blackstone and magma, with fires burning and cracks glowing with lava. There's no rain, only falling ash under a dark sky. Below are huge flat cave halls and lava. It's home to hell toads, blood bats, blazes and, at its heart, a dragon. Go well armed, and remember that you'll need a ship to get there. Danger This is the most dangerous place in the world, and there's no water to drink. Why it's divided like this Look at the lists together and the trade routes are obvious. The Rainlands have the iron but can't feed themselves. The Breadbasket can feed everyone but has almost no metal. Diamonds are on the barren Outer Isles, and every chicken (and every egg) comes from the Spiderholme Isles. See Resources for the full ore picture.

s: Paths wear into the ground where people walk, stone gathers moss, woods reseed themselves and abandoned buildings grow cobwebs.
x: The world changes slowly around you. None of this happens fast, but over weeks the land shows where people live and travel. Paths and roads Wherever people walk, the ground wears. Grass (or podzol, mycelium or rooted dirt) turns to dirt after about a dozen footsteps, then to coarse dirt, which is permanent. Occasional footsteps fade over hours, but a well-used route becomes a real track. Sprinting wears paths faster. Riding a horse wears them twice as fast. Rain doubles the wear on open ground. NPCs and animals wear paths too. Over time, the busy routes between settlements draw themselves on the map. Plants Undergrowth (grass, ferns and tall grass) slowly returns to open ground. In the Caeldun worlds it grows back as the region's own ground cover, so bare hillsides stay bare. Flowers and wildflowers appear now and then and creep outward in patches. Leaf litter gathers under trees. Woods reseed near existing trees, with saplings of the same species. Mushrooms grow in dark, damp places, on stone and wood as well as soil. Seagrass and kelp fill in underwater. Stone and buildings Moss creeps over cobblestone and stone bricks near water. Weathering: stone bricks very slowly crack. Cobwebs gather in dark corners of buildings. They form in built structures only, not in natural caves. Cave moss and dripstone slowly form underground near water. Grass next to fire or lava is scorched to coarse dirt. Weathering weakens Mossy and cracked masonry is structurally weaker than fresh (see Gravity). A stone building near water ages, and a neglected one can eventually fail.

s: Where every ore and cave mineral in the Caeldun Isles is found, drawn from the world generator's own ore rules.
x: Tick ores on and off below the map. Dots mean a trace: dig anywhere there and you'll find a little. Solid colour means rich ground, and the stronger the colour, the more ore per chunk. The map is drawn from the same rules the world generator uses, so it's accurate to the blocks underground. Ore summary Ore Home land Found on Rich on At its richest Iron Rainlands all land (trace) 34.5% ~877 blocks per chunk Coal Northlands all land (trace) 37.4% ~854 blocks per chunk Copper Breadbasket pockets all land (trace) 1.1% ~185 blocks per chunk Quartz Northlands 38.3% 38.3% ~72 blocks per chunk Redstone Outer Isles 20.4% 10.3% ~105 blocks per chunk Diamond Outer Isles 20.4% 9.7% ~81 blocks per chunk Gold Outer Isles 20.4% 0.5% ~48 blocks per chunk Emerald Breadbasket 5.3% 5.3% ~59 blocks per chunk Lapis lazuli Spiderholme Isles 5.3% 5.3% ~56 blocks per chunk "Found on" and "Rich on" are shares of all the land in the world. Cave minerals Mineral Where Rich on Amethyst Veins in Northlands cave walls 6.9% Sulfur and cinnabar Veins in Northlands cave walls 8.4% Lava Deep Northlands caves: the only lava in the world 6.3% Clay Pockets in the pinewoods of Ardveil and Dùnross, surfacing as mud 6.2% Tips for prospectors Dig under high ground. Ores sit in depth bands, and a mountain puts more of the band beneath you. Iron and emerald are richest under hills. Gold is rare in rock: rich on only half a percent of the land. Panning streams is a steadier source. Plan the haul home. A stack of iron blocks weighs 192. See Weight and Ships. See also Resources & ores.

s: Four meters (protein, fruit and veg, grains and thirst) that a varied diet keeps topped up.
h: What goes wrong when you run low
x: On top of the vanilla hunger bar, you have four needs. They show as a bar at the top of the screen whenever you're in a Caeldun world, and /stats prints them in chat. Protein Fruit & veg Grains Thirst How fast they fall Meter Lost per Minecraft day Full to empty Protein 3.5% about 28 days (roughly 9½ hours of play) Fruit & veg 3.5% about 28 days Grains 3.5% about 28 days Thirst 14% about 7 days (roughly 2⅓ hours of play) A Minecraft day is 20 real minutes. Everyone starts at 100%. Thirst Heat makes you thirsty 1.65× faster, in desert, badlands, savanna and jungle biomes. Cold slows thirst to 0.7×, in snowy, frozen and high mountain biomes. Moving adds up to 35% more thirst, depending on how far you travel. Standing in water stops thirst falling and slowly restores it, at about 1% every 10 minutes. That's a trickle, not a drink. Drinks Drink Thirst Also Water bottle +20 Milk bucket +12 +4 protein Honey bottle +4 +2 fruit & veg Carry water Water bottles are by far the best way to stay hydrated. Five of them take you from empty to full. What goes wrong when you run low Effects are driven by whichever meter is lowest. They're checked every 5 seconds. Lowest meter Chance each check Effect 26% or below 12% Brief nausea (3 s) or slowness (5 s) 12% or below 30% Blindness, longer nausea, or strong slowness 5% or below 55% Poison, plus one of the serious effects You'll get a quiet chat warning when a meter crosses a low milestone. Dying Death takes 5% off every meter, but respawning never leaves a meter below 27%. Food values When you eat, a note above your hotbar shows exactly what the food restored. Cooked food is much better than raw, and a stew covers several groups at once. Food Protein Fruit & veg Grains Thirst Cooked beef / porkchop 10 – – – Cooked chicken / mutton / salmon 8 – – – Cooked cod / rabbit 6 – – – Raw beef / porkchop / rabbit 4 – – – Raw chicken / mutton / cod / salmon 3 – – – Rotten flesh 3 – – – Rabbit stew 6 4 3 3 Mushroom stew / suspicious stew 1 7 – 3 Beetroot soup – 8 – 3 Golden carrot – 9 – 1 Golden apple – 8 – 1 Baked potato – 6 – – Apple – 5 – 1 Carrot – 4 – 1 Melon slice – 3 – 2 Sweet berries / glow berries – 3 – 1 Potato (raw) – 2 – – Beetroot – 2 – 1 Dried kelp – 2 – – Bread – – 7 – Pumpkin pie – 4 6 – Cookie – – 4 – Cake (per slice) – 1 3 – Any food not listed spreads its value evenly across protein, fruit and veg, and grains. Where to find each group Grains almost all come from wheat: bread, cookies, pie and cake. Wheat only grows properly in the Breadbasket, so most settlements will need to trade for it. Fruit & veg: potatoes and beetroot grow in every land. Apples drop from oaks. Protein: hunt and fish. Deer, boar, goats and fish are common in the wilder lands. Commands /stats Show your four meters in chat. /needs hud on|off Show or hide the meters bar. It hides by itself while you're riding or sailing.

s: Past the shelf, the sea drops into the abyss. Swimmers and small boats don't survive out there. Ships do.
x: Every island sits on a shallow shelf. Go far enough offshore, usually a few hundred blocks, and the sea floor falls away into the abyss: dark water more than 40 blocks deep. The shallows are turquoise and inviting. The abyss is deep blue and deadly. You can't swim it Over the abyss, anyone swimming gets: Exhaustion: hunger drains fast, about 1.5 points of exhaustion every second. Heavy swimming: constant slowness. Waves that shove you about, and an undertow that sometimes drags you down. Lightning. The storms out here find swimmers; expect a strike about every 30 seconds. Add armour weight (over 30 and you simply sink) and the giant squid, and swimming between islands isn't a plan. Or row it A vanilla boat or raft over the abyss draws the same lightning. You'll lose the boat and probably yourself. Ships are safe Crew aboard a ship built with the Ships system are left alone entirely: no lightning, no waves, no squid. That's the only way across open water, and it's the point. The sea is a barrier until you've built something to cross it. Coastal hopping The shallows around each island are safe to swim and row in. Only the deep water offshore is dangerous, so you can explore your own coast by small boat. What lives out there Creature Behaviour Whales Huge and curious. They swim over to look at you and drift off if you hurt them. They drop blubber. Giant squid Rare and deadly to swimmers: it grabs, damages and drags you under. It can't reach you in a boat or on a ship's deck. Squid herds Squid only live over the abyss. Pufferfish Silent, and best left alone. Sharks Around Dunbarra in the Outer Isles.

s: Swirl a bowl in a shallow gravel stream for gold, iron, flint and sand.
x: Every burn and stream with a gravel bed is a place to pan. It's slow, but it works anywhere in the world and it's the most reliable way to earn your first gold. How to pan Hold a bowl. Find shallow inland water, at most 2 blocks deep, above sea level, over a natural gravel bed. Right-click the water (within 5 blocks). You'll see Panning… above your hotbar. Hold still for 5 seconds. Moving more than a block and a half, or switching away from the bowl, cancels it. What you find Result Chance Gold nugget 2% Iron nugget 1% Flint 7% Sand 90% Your bowl breaks 8% of the time. Each pan has a 15% chance to wear the gravel out, turning it to coarse dirt. Move along the stream when it does. Natural gravel only Gravel you placed yourself doesn't pan, and the sea doesn't either. You're working the stream, not a gravel pile. Sand You can't gather natural sand by hand. Breaking beach sand drops nothing, which keeps the coastline intact. Panning is where sand comes from, and at 90% of results a patient panner can supply a glassworks. Sand you placed yourself can be picked back up as normal. Feathers Not panning, but it's another small source worth knowing: adult chickens drop 2–3 feathers, and wild birds drop 3–6.

s: Which lands hold which ores, how common they are, and how to find them.
x: Ores in the Caeldun Isles are regional. Each land has a low, even spread of its own ores everywhere you dig, plus rich districts where they're concentrated. Outside its home land an ore is a trace at best, and often absent altogether. Ores by land Ore Outer Isles Northlands Spiderholme Breadbasket Rainlands Iron Very slight trace Very rare Very slight trace Extremely rare Rich (vanilla levels) Coal Trace Common Trace Extremely rare Very low Copper Trace Very rare Trace Pockets, and in surface boulders Very low Gold A few rich places, a little everywhere – – – – Diamond Deep – – – – Redstone Deep – – – – Lapis lazuli – Ardcarran only Deep – – Emerald – A little in Ardcarran – Deep – Quartz – Fairly common, all depths – – – Amethyst – Rare veins in caves – – – Sulfur & cinnabar – Rare veins in caves – – – Lava – Deep caves only – – – Clay – Pinewood pockets (showing as mud) – – – "Trace" means you'll turn up the odd block while digging, but you won't supply a settlement from it. Depth matters Ores sit in depth bands, and only the part of a band that's actually underground counts. Mountains give you more rock to dig through before you reach the band's bottom, so iron and emerald country is richest under high ground. Diamond, redstone, lapis and emerald are all deep ores. Other ways to get materials Gold nuggets, iron nuggets, flint and sand come from panning shallow gravel streams. Feathers: chickens drop 2–3; wild birds drop 3–6. Blubber comes from whales in the deep ocean. Timber: whole trees come down when felled. See Tree felling. What this means for you Whatever land you settle in, there'll be things you can't get locally. You can mount an expedition to fetch them, set up an outpost where they are, or trade with someone who already has them. Heavy materials like stone and metal blocks are hard to move without a ship. See Weight. Plan before you build A stone castle is a serious undertaking. The stone has to be quarried, carried or shipped to your site, and then it has to stay up. See Gravity & building.

s: Settlers III is still being built. This is what's on the way.
x: The core of Settlers III is running: regional resources, weight, gravity, ships, nutrition, weather, wildlife and a player economy. Some parts are still being finished. The full map The whole Caeldun Isles map (every region on one continuous world, blended where they meet) has been generated and is being prepared for play. Regions that don't have their own detailed study yet (Fearnmuir, Dùnross, Ruannis, Maigor, Colvane and Ardnamor) take their land's character on the full map. Regional livestock Each land's farm animals (sheep in the Outer Isles, chickens in the Spiderholme Isles, cattle and pigs in the Breadbasket, aurochs in the wild lands) are being settled into place, so bringing animals home by ship becomes part of setting up a farm. The Atlantic rainforest look A custom texture pack is growing to capture the feel of the Atlantic rainforest: ivy-hung oaks, island wildflowers, and the region's own birds and beasts. Parts of it are already in the pack the server sends you. Still being thought through Plenty more is under consideration. If you have ideas, raise them in game with /helpop.

s: Build a ship out of ordinary blocks, fill it with cargo and animals, and sail it smoothly anywhere in the world.
x: Ships are how you cross the sea and move serious cargo. You build one out of normal blocks, however you like, and the server turns it into a vessel that sails smoothly, turns at any angle and docks wherever you drop anchor. Building a ship Build a boat out of blocks, floating in water. Any shape, any materials, up to 2,000 blocks. Give it a hull, a deck, chests for the hold, and a block for the wheel. Look at the block you want as the wheel and run /ship create <name>. That block becomes the helm. Right-click the wheel and choose Set sail. The ship is detected from the wheel outward. Everything connected is part of the ship, up to where it meets the sea floor or land. If it touches the ground you'll get a warning. Make sure it's floating free before you set sail. No building at sea You can't place blocks on a ship while it's under way. Drop anchor first. Sailing Right-click the wheel and Take the wheel. Steer with your movement keys: W/S for throttle, A/D to turn. When you arrive, Drop anchor. The ship turns back into solid blocks wherever she stopped, so you can walk her decks and open her chests like any build. Speed Starts at 4 blocks/second; up to 14 Turn rate 25° per second by default, up to 90° Reverse 40% of forward speed The helm shows your speed and compass heading. Ships leave a wake of spray, and push anything in their path (mobs, players, boats) out of the way. Crew and passengers Anyone standing on deck when the ship sets sail, or who boards her afterwards, is part of the crew. Once she's under way everybody stays seated, skipper included. You can look anywhere, but you can't fall off, be shaken loose, suffocate or drown. Getting off at sea: sneak twice. The first sneak asks if you're sure. Getting on: /ship board, or be aboard when she sails. If the skipper leaves the wheel, the ship drops anchor by herself. Crew on a ship are safe from everything the open ocean throws at swimmers. Cargo Chests, barrels and other containers on board keep their contents for the whole voyage. You can open them at sea, and everything is saved as you go, so even if the server restarts mid-voyage the ship and her cargo come back where she was. Cargo on a ship has no weight penalty for you. That's why ships matter: a hold full of stone or iron would leave you overloaded on foot. Livestock Animals ride along. Cows, sheep, horses, wolves, anything friendly standing on deck when you sail is carried, up to 40 of them. They're protected from harm while aboard and keep grazing and wandering on deck. Pen them in. Animals are only carried while they're over the deck. Fences hold them. Hostile mobs are left behind. Boats and minecarts on deck aren't carried. This is how you bring chickens home from the Spiderholme Isles, or sheep from the Outer Isles. Commands /ship create <name> Make the block you're looking at a ship's wheel. /ship menu Open the wheel menu for the ship you're on. /ship board / /ship leave Join or leave a ship's crew. /ship dock Drop anchor. /ship list Your ships and where they are. /ship remove Stop a build being a ship. The blocks stay where they are. /ship Help.

s: It's the Atlantic: it rains about half the time, in long wet spells and brighter ones, and it usually clears for sunset.
x: The weather in the Caeldun Isles is its own system, not vanilla's occasional storm. It changes often, it rains a lot, and it has a rhythm you'll learn. Spells The weather runs in spells of 10 to 40 minutes. Each spell sets the texture of the weather for a while: Spell How often What it's like Wet spell 4 in 5 Raining about three-quarters of the time, broken by a short sunny gap (around 40 seconds) every few minutes. Bright spell 1 in 5 Mostly sunny, with a quick 15-second shower every four minutes or so. Overall it rains a little over half the time. It's wetter by day and drier at night. The sunset break Most evenings the rain clears about a minute before sunset and stays off for at least three minutes, so you nearly always get to see the sun go down. It happens on about 19 days in 20. Nights Dry stretches last much longer after dark, so nights are the calmest time. Snow Snow falls only on the very highest ground. The snowline sits around Y 285 in the southern mountains and drops about 3 blocks for every kilometre further north. In the northern pinewoods it's about Y 205. Everywhere else, storms bring rain. Storms at sea Out over the abyss, lightning finds swimmers and small boats. See The open ocean. The Burning Isle The burning island never sees rain. Only ash falls there, under a dark sky.

s: Everything you carry has weight. Carry too much and you slow down; wear heavy armour in deep water and you sink.
x: Everything in your inventory weighs something. An ordinary block weighs 1, so a full stack of stone weighs 64. The more you carry, the slower you get. The idea is to make roads, horses and above all ships worth having. Your current load shows as a ⚖ weight bar above your hotbar. Load levels Level Weight Roughly Effect Normal under 120 up to ~2 stacks of blocks None Burdened 120+ ~2 stacks 15% slower Heavy 240+ ~4 stacks 30% slower, 20% lower jumps, no sprinting Overloaded 400+ ~6 stacks 50% slower, no jumping, mining fatigue Shulker boxes don't cheat it A shulker box counts its own weight (5) plus everything inside it. Sinking You sink in water if either of these is true: Your total load is over 400. Your worn armour alone weighs over 30, which is about a full set of iron. So plate armour and deep water don't mix. Cross rivers at fords, build bridges, and take a ship across the sea. Emergency drop If you're going under, sneak and press drop to throw away your heaviest stack in one go. What things weigh Armour (per piece) Material Each piece Full set Leather 2 8 Chainmail 5 20 Iron / gold 8 32 (you sink) Diamond 10 40 Netherite 12 48 Turtle helmet 6 Shield 4 The starter kit (chain helmet and leggings, iron chestplate, leather boots) weighs 20 in armour, safely under the sinking limit. Tools and weapons Material Weight Wooden 2 Stone 3 Iron / gold 4 Diamond 5 Netherite 6 Bow, crossbow, trident 3 Blocks and materials Item Each Stack of 64 Anvil 8 – Gold / diamond / emerald block 4 256 Iron / copper block 3 192 Netherite block 5 320 Any ordinary solid block (stone, planks, dirt…) 1 64 Non-solid blocks (rails, ladders, flowers…) 0.5 32 Wool, leaves, hay bales 0.3 19 Ingots, gems, lapis, quartz 0.5 32 Most other items 0.25 16 Food 0.2 13 Torches 0.2 13 Arrows, string, paper, seeds, redstone, gunpowder 0.1 6 Feathers, saplings, flowers 0.05 3 Moving heavy loads Ships carry whole chests of cargo with no weight penalty. See Ships. Horses and donkeys carry you, and a donkey's chest carries cargo. Roads don't make you lighter, but they make the trip quicker to walk. Carrying money: a gold block weighs 4 and the nine bars it's made of weigh 4.5, so blocks are the lightest way to carry a lot of gold.

s: Each region has its own designed wildlife, from red deer and wolf packs to whales, mosquitoes and the spirits of the high hills.
x: Vanilla's zombies, skeletons and creepers don't roam the Caeldun Isles. Each region has its own roster of creatures that fits the land, the climate and the height. Some are dangerous, some are dinner, and some are just birdsong. Accept the resource pack Many creatures are repainted by the server's resource pack. Without it, a red deer looks like a camel and a mosquito looks like a bee. A creature's name only shows when you look straight at it. The Northlands & Rainlands The wild country of the big islands and peninsulas: forest, moor and mountain. Creature Where Notes Highland wolf Woods and hills Hunts in packs of three. Dangerous. Brown bear Woods, up to the high slopes Big, strong, and not to be fought lightly. Red deer Woods and open hill Skittish; runs from you. Good hunting. Forest boar Woodland Fights back. Wild goat High ground Screams, and unlike vanilla goats, starts the fight. Red fox Woods and edges Wildcat Pinewood (Ardveil) Every untamed cat in the Caeldun Isles is a wildcat. Frogs & newts Lochs, ponds and burns Everywhere near water. Giant bull frog Waterside, Northlands Much bigger than it has any right to be. Wood spider Forest Shore crab Beaches Eagle Overhead Swoops on you like a phantom. Robin, blue tit, goldfinch, greenfinch, herring gull Everywhere Songbirds and gulls. They drop feathers. Spirits of the high ground The higher you climb, the more likely you are to meet things that aren't animals. They're peaceful until provoked. Spirit Notes Forest sprite A small green spirit that throws magick when attacked. Often carries a gold nugget. Wandering soul A lost skeleton, unarmed and unarmoured, that hits very hard once angered. Becomes steadily more common above the treeline. Soul rider A wandering soul on a spectral steed. Rarer, and found higher still. The Outer Isles Creature Notes Wild sheep Flocks on the machair and moor. Wild horse & wild donkey Herds that flee when approached. Worth catching. Rabbit Barren skeleton & skeleton archer Roam the barrens in groups. The archers shoot. Barrens sprite A small drifting ghost of the moors that closes in and strikes. Native huntsman & native shaman The islands' people. Huntsmen shoot arrows and shamans throw fire. They're at war with the bears, wolves and skeletons as well as with you. Brown bear, Highland wolf Fewer than on the mainland. Shark In the waters around Dunbarra. The Spiderholme Isles Creature Notes Black grouse The only chickens in the world: game birds of the fern country. Giant spider Infests the woods of Maigor. Wood spider, songbirds, gulls Whale, giant squid, squid herds In the abyss offshore. See The open ocean. No wolves, no bears. The Breadbasket Tirwenn and Colvane are too small for large animals. There are no bears, wolves or deer, and no hostile humanoids at all. Being warm, they're a breeding ground for smaller things. Creature Notes Mosquito & mosquito swarms Tiger-striped and bloodthirsty. They bite as they fly past. Midge swarms A west-coast summer in one creature. Shore crab, rock crab Beaches and rocks.
